subject: biochemistry
title: Amino acids and protein structure: essentials, zwitterions, folding and misfolding

steps.tx: Ten amino acids are nutritionally **essential** and must come from diet (PVT TIM HALL: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, arginine, leucine, lysine). Of these, **histidine** and **arginine** are semi-essential, since adults synthesise small amounts. The three **branched chain** amino acids are valine, leucine and isoleucine. Tyrosine is non-essential because it is made from phenylalanine, as are proline, alanine and glutamate.
steps.say: Ten amino acids are nutritionally essential and must come from the diet: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, arginine, leucine and lysine. Histidine and arginine are semi-essential. The three branched chain amino acids are valine, leucine and isoleucine. Tyrosine is non-essential because it is made from phenylalanine.

steps.tx: Amino acids are glucogenic, ketogenic or both. Glucogenic amino acids feed gluconeogenesis through pyruvate or TCA intermediates. Ketogenic amino acids such as leucine and lysine form acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA. Tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine and isoleucine are both. Tryptophan is essential and a precursor of **niacin**, **serotonin** and melatonin. Tryptophan also absorbs UV light near 280 nm, so it strongly affects a protein's absorbance.
steps.say: Amino acids are glucogenic, ketogenic or both. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic. Tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine and isoleucine are both. Tryptophan is essential and gives rise to niacin, serotonin and melatonin. Its aromatic ring is the main reason proteins absorb light near 280 nanometres.

steps.tx: Peptide bonds link amino acids through a covalent bond between the carboxyl carbon and the amino nitrogen. The **primary structure** is this linear sequence. The **alpha helix** is stabilised by hydrogen bonds along the backbone, while the **beta pleated sheet** uses hydrogen bonds between neighbouring strands. Proline cannot donate a hydrogen bond, so it breaks helices and creates kinks. Glycine is flexible and also disrupts helices. Secondary structure is mostly held by hydrogen bonds, while tertiary and quaternary structures depend on hydrophobic, ionic and disulfide interactions.
steps.say: Peptide bonds are covalent links that form the primary structure. The alpha helix is held by hydrogen bonds along its backbone, and the beta pleated sheet uses hydrogen bonds between strands. Proline cannot donate a hydrogen bond, so it breaks helices and creates kinks. Glycine is also disruptive because of its flexibility. Tertiary and quaternary structure depend on other bonds.

steps.tx: Use this checklist before the exam, focusing on **carnosine**, a dipeptide built from beta alanine and **histidine** that is found in muscle. **Sarcosine** is an N methyl derivative of glycine. Non covalent interactions rank: ionic bonds, then **hydrogen bonds**, then **van der Waals forces**, which are the weakest. **Calnexin** is a chaperone that assists folding of exported glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. **Alpha-1 antitrypsin** is synthesised in the liver. **Trypsin** cuts peptide chains after lysine and arginine residues.
steps.say: Before the exam, make sure you can recall a handful of facts. Carnosine is a dipeptide made from beta alanine and histidine, and it is found in muscle. Sarcosine is N methyl glycine. Non covalent interactions rank ionic bonds first, then hydrogen bonds, then van der Waals forces, which are the weakest. Calnexin helps fold proteins as they enter the secretory pathway. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is made in the liver. Trypsin cleaves after lysine and arginine.
